question: What does Morgan Stanley pay its financial advisors?

claims.text: The 2025 10-K (published 2026-02-19) states that for certain revenue-producing employees in Wealth Management and Investment Management, compensation is largely paid on the basis of formulaic payouts that link employee compensation to revenues.

The 2025 10-K (published 2026-02-19) states that Morgan Stanley sponsors deferred cash-based and stock-based compensation programs that include Wealth Management financial advisors, and that these generally contain vesting, clawback and cancellation provisions. It says deferred compensation for Wealth Management financial advisors is generally composed of 75% cash-based awards and 25% stock-based awards. Employees can allocate deferred cash awards among a firm-selected menu of notional investments (fixed income, equity, commodity and money market funds).

The June 2026 10-Q (published 2026-08-04) repeats the 75% cash / 25% stock composition of Wealth Management advisor deferred compensation. It says compensation expense for deferred cash awards is based on the notional award value, adjusted for changes in the fair value of the investments employees select, and is recognized over the vesting period.

The 3Q26 financial supplement (published 2026-10-14) says that beginning in the first quarter of 2026, hedges for Wealth Management deferred cash-based compensation awards were primarily transitioned to derivative instruments. As a result, the firm no longer presents non-GAAP measures of net revenues and compensation expense excluding DCP.

adjacent.text: The 2025 10-K (published 2026-02-19) reports firm-wide compensation and benefits expense of $29,216 million in 2025, up 12%. It attributes the rise primarily to an increase in the formulaic payout to Wealth Management advisors and higher discretionary incentive compensation within Institutional Securities, both on higher revenues, and to higher salary expenses.
adjacent.differs_because: Aggregate compensation expense covers all employees and pay types; it is not the advisor payout grid.

adjacent.text: The June 2026 10-Q (published 2026-08-04) says Wealth Management compensation and benefits expenses increased primarily as a result of an increase in the formulaic payout to Wealth Management advisors driven by higher compensable revenues. No payout rate is given.
adjacent.differs_because: Aggregate compensation expense covers all employees and pay types; it is not the advisor payout grid.

adjacent.text: InvestmentNews (published 2026-10-26) reported that Morgan Stanley is increasing a pay threshold for advisors by 10% in 2027, meaning advisors have to generate that much more revenue to see the same pay. It also reported that Morgan Stanley and Merrill Lynch are not introducing retention bonuses in their 2027 pay plans. The article describes large firms like Morgan Stanley as having taken a small amount of an advisor's gross revenue as deferred compensation that advisors must stay for years to vest, with forfeiture on departure.
adjacent.differs_because: Trade-press reporting is indicative, not authoritative.

adjacent.text: InvestmentNews (published 2026-08-28) reported that Morgan Stanley sued a former advisor in 2021 over promissory notes (loans brokers pay back to firms over time) and sought to claw back recruiting bonus money. This indicates that recruiting bonuses exist, but it gives no terms.
adjacent.differs_because: Trade-press reporting is indicative, not authoritative.

gaps.what: Payout grids are not public. The evidence gives no payout percentages or grid tiers, no commission or fee-based payout rates, no bonus amounts, and no average or aggregate advisor pay figures for Morgan Stanley Wealth Management.
gaps.suggested_source: Morgan Stanley Wealth Management advisor compensation plan documents or recruiting disclosures; industry compensation surveys
